observationsAndConclusions.why: The relation is about how the elements fit together rather than about how many there are, so the shape can change while the combination does not
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Every solid counted gives a different set of three numbers, and the same value for faces plus vertices less edges
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A quantity that stays put while everything feeding it changes is worth conjecturing about

observationsAndConclusions.why: Some edges lie behind the solid and are drawn dashed, and a dashed edge is an edge of the solid all the same
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A count taken without stepping the view comes out short of the true edge count
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: What a drawing hides is not missing from the object, so counting has to reach the elements the view does not show

observationsAndConclusions.why: Three cases are the evidence that suggested the rule, so they cannot also be the evidence that tests it
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Three solids agreeing does not settle the relation, and a fourth solid that was never counted does more work than all three
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A conjecture earns its keep on a case it has not already been fitted to

media.description: One polyhedron stands in a fixed isometric projection with its rear edges drawn dashed, the NCERT convention, and three counters beside it. Tapping a face, an edge or a vertex fills or thickens it permanently and ticks the matching counter in the same moment, so nothing is counted twice and nothing is lost; a counted element is not offered a second time, and only the elements the current view actually shows can be reached. Four fixed views turn the solid without any free rotation, carrying every highlight with them, which is how the dashed rear edges and the underside are reached - and on a wide, short pane all four are drawn side by side, so the class can see the same solid with the dashed edges moving from one drawing to the next. A table collects faces, edges and vertices for every solid counted so far, one row per solid, and prints the combination beside them; the columns differ from row to row while the combination does not. A relation can be picked from the four the tool knows and run on a solid whose row is NOT in the table, with the substitution shown on screen as arithmetic rather than reported as a verdict, so a wrong relation is refuted by a named solid with its own counts rather than by a cross. A cylinder can be offered and is refused with the reason stated, because the definitions in use are for flat faces.

source_tool.description: The student counts faces, edges and vertices for several solids and finds the relation that holds for all of them.

modes.ai: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with a cube and the counts HIDDEN, and asks whether there is a rule connecting the three. Beat 2 counts a cube and a prism, filling the table. Beat 3 takes the class's conjectured relation and tests it on a pyramid they have not counted. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setSolid, countElement, testRelation and say. No drag: the agent counts by naming elements.
modes.learn: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets the solid from its own key, shows the question, then reveals the counts, the table and the relation together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
modes.normal: Free Play, student operated. The student picks any solid, taps elements to count them, steps the view, and tests any relation. Nothing is scored and nothing is mandatory.
modes.practice: Practice, student operated. The bank from props.questions, one item at a time, each rendering its own solid. Give one of the three counts, give a missing value from the other two, or state the relation. Scored, with a star finish and a Review phase that walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer and the counted table.

theme.premise: A class is asked whether the three counts of a solid are connected at all, and four solids are counted one element at a time to find out
theme.setting: A plain working ground with one solid drawn in a fixed isometric projection, hidden edges dashed, and three counters standing beside it, one for faces, one for edges and one for vertices
theme.visualStyle: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration
theme.studentPalette: The warmer accent of the same family, with the score and the Finish button carrying it
theme.teacherPalette: The cool indigo accent, low chrome, high contrast, so a projected board stays readable

practice.rating: all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1, never 0
practice.review: The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer, and the counted table.

scenes.onScreen: The solid, the stepper, the counters, the table, every control, no score and no question. A cube with nothing counted and every control live.
scenes.animation: Element count: the tapped element fills and its counter ticks in the same moment, so the tap and the count are one act.
scenes.interaction: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.
scenes.valuesShown: Every readout stays live, so the invariants keep being computed while the student explores

concept.notation: Faces are the flat surfaces, edges the lines where two faces meet, and vertices the points where edges meet. The relation is written as faces plus vertices minus edges.
concept.statement: For every solid with flat faces, the number of faces plus the number of vertices is two more than the number of edges. Counting a cube, a prism and a pyramid gives different numbers in each column but the same value for that combination, which is why the relation is worth conjecturing.
misconceptions: Hidden edges not counted, so the totals come out short.
The relation assumed to depend on the solid's shape rather than holding generally.
concept.why_it_is_true: Each solid is stored as an explicit list of faces, edges and vertices, so the counts are exact whatever the drawing shows. Testing a conjectured relation on a solid the student has not counted is what turns a pattern across three cases into a claim, and a wrong relation fails on a specific solid rather than being marked wrong.
worked_numbers: A cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices, and 6 plus 8 minus 12 is 2.
A triangular prism has 5, 9 and 6, and 5 plus 6 minus 9 is 2.
A square pyramid has 5, 8 and 5, and 5 plus 5 minus 8 is 2.

stepViewOutcomes.0: the opening fixed angle, where the rear edges are dashed

stepViewOutcomes.2: an angle from which the previously hidden edges are solid and reachable
stepViewOutcomes.3: the last fixed angle, after which the stepper returns to 0

showTableOutcomes.on: every solid counted so far is listed with its three counts on one row

testRelationOutcomes.F plus V is E: is short by exactly 2 on every solid, which is the near miss worth naming
testRelationOutcomes.F times V is E: fails on the cube, giving 48 against 12
testRelationOutcomes.F plus E is V plus 2: fails on the cube at once, giving 18 against 10
testRelationOutcomes.F plus V is E plus 2: holds on every solid in the bank, including the one that has not been counted

answer_key.worked: For every solid counted, faces plus vertices minus edges is 2.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the solid's stored lists: each count, a missing value from the other two, and whether a typed relation holds.
answer_key.precision: Each solid is stored as explicit face, edge and vertex lists, so counting and rendering share one source and no element can be missed or double counted.
answer_key.ground_truth: counts(solid) = the lengths of its three lists. relationValue(solid) = faces plus vertices minus edges. relationHolds(text, solid) = the typed relation evaluated on the stored counts.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Brought into view by the stepped view control, since the count must include them; the tool never counts an element the student cannot see.
Impossible by construction, since tapped elements stay highlighted and the highlight state enforces single counting.
Tested on a fourth unseen solid, so a pattern across three is not accepted as a rule.
Refuted by a specific solid with its counts shown, rather than by a mark.

edge_cases.case: A solid with a curved surface
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Excluded from the bank with the reason stated, since faces and edges are defined here for flat surfaces.

hostProps.additionalProps.exampleSeed: A 32 bit int the tool's mulberry32 PRNG consumes directly. The teacher agent builds its own copy of the example set from the SAME seed, so Math.random(), Date.now() or ignoring the seed desynchronises the narration from the screen in every single session.

questions.description: Replaces the built in practice bank. Items are {kind:'count', solid:string, element:string} | {kind:'missing', solid:string, given:object} | {kind:'state_relation'} | {kind:'choice', prompt, options[], correct, explain}.

showTable.description: Show the counted table across solids. Off until a prediction is committed.

constraints: An element cannot be counted twice, enforced by highlight state rather than by a running check.
Each solid is stored as explicit face, edge and vertex lists, so counting and rendering share one source.
Views are stepped only, with no free rotation, since there is no 3D engine.
A conjectured relation is tested on a solid the student has not counted, so three agreeing cases do not close the stage.
Solids with curved surfaces are excluded from the bank with the reason stated.

extra.concept_only: Concept carries no questions of its own. Its beats reveal the idea and then run one reasoning beat each, and every number the agent says is read from state.truth.

ai.shows: The solid in isometric projection, the view stepper, the three counters, the table, the teacher caption, and discrete step navigation (Prev / Step k of 3 / Next) with a progress bar.
steps: Predict: a cube is shown with all three counts HIDDEN. The class commits whether a rule connects them, out loud, and the teacher commits it on the pad. prediction_made unlocks the beat.
Count: the cube and then a prism are counted element by element, filling the table.
Test: the conjectured relation is run on a pyramid nobody has counted.
ai.done_when: Beat 3 has been reached and the relation has been tested on an uncounted solid. Concept has no Finish button.

normal.shows: The solid, the stepper, the counters, the table, every control, no score and no question.
steps: No steps. Nothing is mandatory and nothing is scored.
normal.done_when: The student presses Finish, which emits finished once.
normal.opens_with: A cube with nothing counted and every control live.
play_modes: HIDDEN EDGE HUNT: count a solid from one view, step the view, and say which elements you had missed.
BREAK A RELATION: invent a relation that fits the cube, then hunt for the solid that kills it.
FOURTH SOLID: read a relation off three solids, then test it on one you have not counted.
FAMILY EDGE: try a solid with a curved surface and say why the counters refuse it.
normal.parameter_freedom: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example testing a relation a child proposes on a solid nobody has counted.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to make the count HONEST before it is made interesting. Ask the class to count the cube's edges out loud from the drawing before you say anything - they will say 9, because three of them are behind the solid. The screen has all twelve highlighted with the rear three dashed, so the gap between what they said and what is lit is the lesson, and it costs one sentence.

Beat 2 is the whole argument in one screen. The prism's three numbers are all different from the cube's - 7, 15 and 10 against 6, 12 and 8 - and the table puts them one under the other so the class can see three columns change while a fourth does not. Point at the columns first and the last column second; that order is what makes the constant worth conjecturing about.

Beat 3 turns the observation into a claim, and the important thing on screen is what is MISSING: the pyramid has no row in the table, because nobody counted it. Run the relation on it and the substitution lands as arithmetic the class can follow. Then read the red line - the same three counts, arranged wrongly, fail on the cube at once - so a wrong relation is settled by a named solid rather than by being marked wrong.

media.context: This hook opens the topic on faces, edges and vertices. Students can read views. The film must not state the relationship and must not give the three counts for the cube.
media.description: Sketch a cube from one angle and try to count its corners, its edges and its flat faces, and it is easy to miss the ones hiding round the back. There is a surprising check that ties the three counts together every single time.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Count faces, edges and vertices of a solid and use the relationship between them. Key teaching points: 1) Faces, edges and vertices can all be counted for a flat sided solid. 2) Hidden parts must be included in the count. 3) Faces plus vertices minus edges always gives two. 4) Prisms and pyramids have their own formulas in terms of the base. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often count only the visible faces of a drawn solid. 2) Students often confuse edges with faces. Pause points: 0:25, at the end of a tidy bookkeeping: ask how many faces a cube has, including the hidden ones. 0:25, just before the open question: ask what the three counts might have to do with each other. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask how many edges a cube has. After viewing, ask what a check would be worth here.

topics.summary: Solids with flat faces are described by faces, edges and vertices, with F + V - E always equal to 2, and prisms and pyramids on an n-sided base follow simple count formulas. The learner counts features and predicts counts for any base.

content.text: A solid with flat surfaces is described by its faces (the flat surfaces), its edges (the lines where two faces meet), and its vertices (the points where edges meet). A cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. When you count from one picture, some edges and vertices hide behind the solid, so you must turn the solid to catch them all. A useful check is Euler's relation: for these solids, the number of faces plus the number of vertices, minus the number of edges, always comes to 2. So F + V - E = 2. For a cube, 6 + 8 - 12 = 2. This check catches a miscount, and it lets you find a missing count when you know the other two.

content.text: A prism is named by its base polygon: a triangular prism, a pentagonal prism, and so on. On an n-sided base it has a top face, a bottom face and n side faces, so F = n + 2. Its edges come in three groups, a top ring of n, a bottom ring of n, and n verticals joining them, so E = 3n. Its vertices are the n top corners and n bottom corners, so V = 2n. A pyramid on an n-sided base has the base plus n triangular faces, so F = n + 1; its edges are the n base edges and n slanted edges to the apex, so E = 2n; and its vertices are the n base corners plus the apex, so V = n + 1. These formulas let you predict the counts for any n, even a 100-sided base.

A pyramid on an n-sided base has the base plus n triangular faces, so F = n + 1; its edges are the n base edges and n slanted edges to the apex, so E = 2n; and its vertices are the n base corners plus the apex, so V = n + 1. These formulas let you predict the counts for any n, even a 100-sided base.

topics.brief_summary: Solids with flat faces are described by faces, edges and vertices, with F + V - E always equal to 2, and prisms and pyramids on an n-sided base follow simple count formulas. The learner counts features and predicts counts for any base.
topics.original_chunk: A solid with flat surfaces is described by its faces (the flat surfaces), its edges (the lines where two faces meet), and its vertices (the points where edges meet). A cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. When you count from one picture, some edges and vertices hide behind the solid, so you must turn the solid to catch them all. A useful check is Euler's relation: for these solids, the number of faces plus the number of vertices, minus the number of edges, always comes to 2. So F + V - E = 2. For a cube, 6 + 8 - 12 = 2. This check catches a miscount, and it lets you find a missing count when you know the other two. learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer how flat surfaces, meeting lines and corner points describe a solid, and determine that a face is a flat surface, an edge is where two faces meet, and a vertex is where edges meet, hidden ones included. They will explain that for such solids the number of faces plus vertices minus edges always equals 2, and predict a missing count from the other two.
Examine the worked examples of counting faces, edges and vertices, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving counting faces, edges and vertices, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer how the counts of a prism or a pyramid depend on the base polygon, and determine that a prism on an n-sided base has n plus 2 faces, 3n edges and 2n vertices, while a pyramid has n plus 1 faces, 2n edges and n plus 1 vertices. They will explain why naming a solid by its base predicts these counts for any base size without building it.

media.generation_prompt: Flat educational vector illustration in the style of an NCERT Grade 8 mathematics textbook: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines, a restrained palette of one teal accent, one amber accent and neutral grey, flat fills with no shading and no gradients, all wording in a clean sans-serif, 16:9 landscape at 1456 by 816 pixels. Scene: The cross net is drawn at the left, a row of four squares with one square above the second and one below the second, with its six squares numbered. A folding sequence in three small stages shows it closing into a cube, with each square landing on a distinct face and a completed cube drawn with all six faces accounted for, ticked. To the right, a failing arrangement of six squares is drawn, crossed, with a folding attempt showing two squares landing on the same face and one face left uncovered, both marked. A rule card at the foot reads that six squares are not enough; they must cover all six faces exactly once. Draw no wording at all except the following, which is the complete and only text in the figure, spelled exactly like this: 1; 2; 3; 4; 5; 6; the cross net; folds into a cube; two squares on one face; one face left uncovered; six squares are not enough.
media.accuracy_constraints:
The cross net must have exactly six squares in the arrangement described.
The folding sequence must land each square on a distinct cube face, covering all six.
The failing arrangement must genuinely double up on a face and leave one uncovered, and must be crossed.
All squares must be drawn equal in size.
The rule must state that six squares alone do not guarantee a net.
Every number, count and label drawn in the figure must match this brief exactly; no value may be invented, rounded or added.
Use NCERT Ganita Prakash Grade 8 wording for every term, keep British spelling, and write no sentence that a Grade 8 reader could not read aloud.

media.title: Cube Net Sorter
media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Visualising Solid Shapes - nets of a cube, revising the nets met in Class 7. The tool is read where spatial judgement is measured before it is corrected: the class sorts by eye first, and folding is unlocked afterwards to see how that judgement did. It carries the textbook's own instruction to answer by visualisation before cutting out, and it never states a run-length rule or the count of 11 as a fact to recite - the count is reached in Free Play by testing.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's prediction, the fold result and the collision that settles it.

overview.goal: The student sorts candidate nets into folds and does not fold, states a reason for each rejection, and builds a valid net of their own.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground with candidate six square arrangements laid out as cards, two labelled bins above them and a folding panel below where one card at a time is put to the test. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class sorts the cards by how tidy they look, and the folding panel is unlocked afterwards to see how that judgement did.
overview.concept: Not every arrangement of six squares folds into a cube. Folding succeeds only when the six squares land on the six cube faces exactly once, and fails when two of them would land on the same face. Judging by symmetry or neatness does not work, which is why the prediction has to be made before folding.
overview.purpose: The student sorts candidate nets into folds and does not fold, states a reason for each rejection, and builds a valid net of their own.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Bins across the upper main panel, card table beneath, fold panel below that. On a 390 px frame the table scrolls and every card keeps a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not allow folding before every card is sorted, and never hard code the valid net list. Folding early would remove the prediction the tool exists to measure.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Folding maps each square to a cube face. Since a cube has six faces and a net has six squares, a valid net is exactly one where that map is a bijection. Any arrangement where two squares reach the same face leaves another face uncovered, and the collision is where that shows up. Simulating the fold on a cube coordinate lattice settles it for any arrangement, including one a student invents. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the cards face up and both bins EMPTY, and instructs that every card must be placed before anything is folded. Beat 2 sorts the obvious cases by prediction. Beat 3 folds each card in turn, and a rejected one shows the two faces that would land on the same place. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with placeCard, foldCheck, buildNet and say. No drag: the agent places a card by naming its bin.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open with the cards face up, both bins empty and folding locked, and ask the class to place every card by judgement alone. Commit each class decision as its card is placed. Targets all the cards sorted with folding still locked. Never fold anything at this call, however confident the class is about a card. Call 2. Unlock folding and fold each card in turn so the tally fills as the predictions are marked. Point at the tally and then at the card that has just folded. Targets the folding of every sorted card. Read the tally and each result from getState().truth, never from this plan. Call 3. Take one rejected card and hold the two squares that land on the same face, so the failure has a place on the card. Targets the near miss card in the folding panel with the colliding pair shown. Name which pair collides and which face is left uncovered, and read the pair from getState().truth.

hunts: TIDY FAILURE: find the neatest arrangement you can that does not fold, and name the pair that collides.
RAGGED SUCCESS: find the most awkward looking arrangement that does fold, and say why looks did not decide it.
ONE SQUARE MOVE: take an arrangement that fails and move one square so that it folds.
REASON CHECK: reject a card, write your reason, then fold it and see whether the collision matches.

observationsAndConclusions.why: Folding depends on where the squares sit relative to one another, and symmetry is a fact about the drawing rather than about the fold
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Cards that look neat and symmetric turn out to fold no more reliably than awkward looking ones
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A judgement has to be checked against the thing it claims to predict, and here that thing is the fold

observationsAndConclusions.why: Six squares are being sent to six faces, so the moment two of them share a face there is a face nothing reaches
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Every rejected card ends with exactly two squares meeting at the same place
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A rejection can always be located, which turns does not fold into a statement about a particular pair

observationsAndConclusions.why: The near miss keeps the shape and the square count of a valid net and changes only the relation the fold depends on
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A card that differs from a good net by moving one square is often the hardest to judge
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Small changes to an arrangement can flip the answer, so a rule of thumb about appearance cannot be trusted

media.description: Six candidate arrangements of squares stand in two labelled bins with folding locked, so the whole judgement is on record before any of it is tested. Unlocking the fold rolls a cube across each arrangement square by square, and every square takes the colour of the cube face it lands on - so a valid net ends up wearing six different colours, and a rejected one wears the same colour twice. That repeated colour IS the collision: the two squares are ringed and linked, one of the six face pips carries a 2, another is left empty and dashed, and a see-through isometric cube beside the card shows the doubled face tinted and the bare face untouched. Nothing about a card's verdict is stored: every arrangement, including one a student builds square by square on the grid, is judged by the same rolling-cube simulation, which is why the tool can tell a tidy symmetric arrangement that fails from a ragged staircase that folds.

concept.notation: A net folds into a cube when its six squares cover the six cube faces exactly once. Having six squares is necessary but not sufficient.
concept.statement: Not every arrangement of six squares folds into a cube. Folding succeeds only when the six squares land on the six cube faces exactly once, and fails when two of them would land on the same face. Judging by symmetry or neatness does not work, which is why the prediction has to be made before folding.
prerequisites: how a net folds into a solid
the six faces of a cube
misconceptions: Nets judged by symmetry or neatness rather than by folding.
The number of valid cube nets guessed rather than reasoned.
concept.why_it_is_true: Folding maps each square to a cube face. Since a cube has six faces and a net has six squares, a valid net is exactly one where that map is a bijection. Any arrangement where two squares reach the same face leaves another face uncovered, and the collision is where that shows up. Simulating the fold on a cube coordinate lattice settles it for any arrangement, including one a student invents.
worked_numbers: Eleven distinct arrangements of six squares fold into a cube.
A T shaped arrangement with an extra square on the wrong arm collides on one face.
A two by three block leaves two faces uncovered.

answer_key.worked: A net folds into a cube exactly when its six squares cover the six cube faces once each; a collision means one face is covered twice and another not at all.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime by simulating the fold: the validity flag per net and the colliding face pair when invalid.
answer_key.precision: Validation simulates the fold on a cube coordinate lattice and checks that each of the six cube faces is covered exactly once. The known valid net list is never hard coded.
answer_key.ground_truth: foldsToCube(net) = every cube face covered exactly once after simulation. collision(net) = the pair of squares landing on the same face, when there is one.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Refused as a net at all, with the reason stated, since a net must fold from one piece.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

visual_behaviour.never: Do not allow folding before every card is sorted, and never hard code the valid net list. Folding early would remove the prediction the tool exists to measure.
visual_behaviour.scene: Candidate six square arrangements drawn as cards on a grid, sorted into two labelled bins. A folded card shows its cube in fixed isometric projection; a rejected one shows the two colliding squares tinted in the warning tone with a link between them.
visual_behaviour.layout: Bins across the upper main panel, card table beneath, fold panel below that. On a 390 px frame the table scrolls and every card keeps a 44 px hit target.

The tally of correct predictions, once folding has run
For a rejected card, the colliding pair
animations: Fold: faces hinge up as two dimensional shears towards the isometric view, so folding is drawn without a 3D engine.
Collision: the two offending squares meet and are held overlapping for a moment, so the failure is located rather than reported.
Tally fill: each prediction is marked right or wrong as its card folds, so judgement is scored card by card.
visual_behaviour.scale_rule: Card size is derived from the panel width so every six square arrangement is legible and keeps a 44 px hit target; the table scrolls rather than shrinking cards.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to put an appearance-based judgement on record before any evidence arrives. The bins open holding the sort a class actually makes - the tidy Block and the near miss in 'Folds', the ragged Staircase in 'Does not fold' - and folding is locked. Do not fold anything at this beat, however confident the class is.

Beat 2 is the whole argument in one motion. Every card colours in at once and the tally lands on 2 of 6: the Cross and the One row were judged right, and the Block, the Near miss and the Staircase were all judged wrong. The Staircase is the one to point at - the ugliest card on screen is one of the two that folds.

Beat 3 turns 'it does not fold' into a place. The Near miss keeps the square count and roughly the shape of a good net and changes only the relation the fold depends on, so its collision - row 1 column 4 with row 3 column 2 - is what the class names. Say the two halves together: one face covered twice IS one face left bare.

Build your own six square arrangement on the grid and fold it. 8. In Practice, answer each item and press Finish when the bank is done.

media.title: Will This Flat Shape Fold Into a Box
media.context: This hook opens the topic on nets of a cube. Students can count faces. The film must not give the number of distinct nets and must not say how to tell a winner from a dud.
media.description: Cut six paper squares and lay them in a row, or a cross, or a staircase. Some of these flat arrangements fold neatly into a closed cube and some jam, leaving two faces on top of each other or a gap where a face should be.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Decide which arrangements of six squares fold into a cube. Key teaching points: 1) A net must have exactly six squares. 2) The arrangement decides whether it closes. 3) A jam shows two faces landing in the same place. 4) There are eleven genuinely different nets of a cube. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often assume any six connected squares form a net. 2) Students often count reflections and rotations as different nets. Pause points: 0:24, at the end of and some jam: ask which of the three arrangements will fold. 0:24, just before the open question: ask how many nets the class expects. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what goes wrong in a net that jams. After viewing, ask how they would test one without folding it.

topics.summary: A net is a solid unfolded flat; only certain arrangements of squares fold into a cube, and a cube has 11 distinct nets while a tetrahedron has 2. The learner predicts fold or fail and counts the distinct nets.

content.text: A net is a solid unfolded flat. To fold into a cube, an arrangement must have six squares that, when folded, cover all six cube faces exactly once. Having six squares is not enough. A cross (a row of four squares with one above and one below) folds. So do several staircase shapes. But a 2 by 3 rectangle, a straight row of six, and any shape holding a solid 2 by 2 block all fail, because folding makes two faces overlap or leaves a face open. Counting every arrangement that folds, treating a rotation or a flip as the same, a cube has exactly 11 distinct nets. A regular tetrahedron has only 2, and a regular octahedron has 11, like the cube.

media.title: Net Folder
media.context: CBSE Class 8, Visualising Solid Shapes: nets, folding, which faces meet, and the counting that follows. It opens the solids thread of the chapter, so everything later about views, isometric drawings and counting depends on the flat and folded pictures being connected here. The grade's own relations are what the tool computes with: an n-gonal prism has n+2 faces, 3n edges and 2n vertices; an n-gonal pyramid has n+1 faces, 2n edges and n+1 vertices; a net of F faces has F-1 fold lines and its remaining boundary glues in E-(F-1) pairs. NCERT's own fact that only 11 of the 35 six-square arrangements fold to a cube is what the collision case exists to make visible.

overview.goal: The student predicts which solid a net folds into, marks which faces will meet, and checks both by folding.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground with a flat net lying on a light grid, its fold lines dashed, and the solid appearing in the same area as the faces hinge up towards a fixed isometric view. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class is asked which solid a net makes and which of its faces will end up touching, and both answers are committed before a single fold is made.
overview.concept: A net folds into a solid by hinging each face up about its fold lines. Faces that end up sharing an edge on the solid are the ones that meet, and a net that would make two faces collide cannot close. Tracing a face between the flat and folded views is what keeps the two pictures connected.
overview.purpose: The student predicts which solid a net folds into, marks which faces will meet, and checks both by folding.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Net fills the main panel with the emerging solid appearing in the same area as folds complete. On a 390 px frame the net rescales rather than scrolling, and every fold line keeps a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not reveal the solid while a prediction is still open, and never complete a fold that causes a collision. Completing it would hide the failure the flag exists to show.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Folding preserves each face exactly; only its position changes. So the solid's faces are the net's faces rearranged, and which ones end up adjacent is determined by the net's own adjacency. A collision means two faces are being sent to the same place, which no fold can resolve, and flagging it before the fold completes shows the failure at the point it arises. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open with the net lying flat, nothing folded and no solid shown, and ask the class to say out loud which solid it makes. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Targets the net at zero folds. Never fold a line before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Fold the lines one at a time so each face hinges up unchanged, tracing one named face in both views as it goes. Point at the traced face in the flat net and then at the same face on the solid. Targets the base traced through the first four folds. Read the fold counter and the traced face from getState().truth, never from this plan. Call 3. Before the last folds, ask the class to name a pair of faces that will meet, mark it, and complete the fold so the mark is confirmed or refuted. Targets a marked meeting between the front face and the right side face. Say which pair met and which did not, and read the result from getState().truth.

hunts: MEETING PAIR: mark two faces you think will meet, then fold and see whether they did.
COLLISION HUNT: build an arrangement that collides, and say which pair goes to the same place.
HALF FOLD: stop halfway and trace one face back to where it started on the flat net.
UNFOLD TEST: fold fully, unfold, and check that every face is back exactly where it began.

media.description: A flat net lies on a light working ground with its fold lines drawn in their own colour, and the solid it makes stands beside it in fixed isometric projection. Folding is exact rather than illustrative: a cube is rolled square by square across the net, so the tool knows which cube face every square becomes, which two squares end up opposite, and which two are being sent to the same place. Each face travels from its own flat position into its place on the solid while its outline stays drawn where it started, and the isometric edge is scaled by one over the square root of cos 30 so a drawn face rhombus has exactly the flat square's area — the class can see that folding moves a face without changing it. A net that cannot close stops mid fold with the two offending faces tinted and, in the same frame, the cube face nobody reached outlined and labelled left empty, because overlap on its own reads as a near miss. Every fold line is tappable with a 44 pixel target and reverses exactly, so a partly folded net is a state the tool draws rather than an unfinished one. The read-out band carries the faces, the edges, the vertices, the fold lines and the glued pairs, and a count that belongs to the solid reads a dash rather than a number whenever the net cannot close. Nets of prisms and pyramids on up to a twelve sided family are drawn the same way, and a net above the twelve face cap is refused with the cap named on screen rather than failing silently.

concept.notation: A fold line is an edge between two faces of the net. Two faces meet when folding brings their edges together on the solid.
concept.statement: A net folds into a solid by hinging each face up about its fold lines. Faces that end up sharing an edge on the solid are the ones that meet, and a net that would make two faces collide cannot close. Tracing a face between the flat and folded views is what keeps the two pictures connected.
prerequisites: faces and edges of a solid
misconceptions: Any six square arrangement assumed to fold into a cube.
Faces not tracked between the flat and folded views, so the solid is recognised without being understood.
concept.why_it_is_true: Folding preserves each face exactly; only its position changes. So the solid's faces are the net's faces rearranged, and which ones end up adjacent is determined by the net's own adjacency. A collision means two faces are being sent to the same place, which no fold can resolve, and flagging it before the fold completes shows the failure at the point it arises.
worked_numbers: A cross shaped net of six squares folds into a cube.
Its two arm ends meet as opposite faces.
An arrangement where two squares would land together is flagged before the fold finishes.

predictSolidOutcomes.cuboid: six rectangles in three matching pairs fold to a cuboid with the same counts as a cube
predictSolidOutcomes.prismOn5: two 5 sided faces and 5 rectangles fold to a prism with 7 faces, 15 edges and 10 vertices
predictSolidOutcomes.prismOn6: two 6 sided faces and 6 rectangles fold to a prism with 8 faces, 18 edges and 12 vertices
predictSolidOutcomes.pyramidOn7: one 7 sided face and 7 triangles fold to a pyramid with 8 faces, 14 edges and 8 vertices
predictSolidOutcomes.cannotClose: the fold halts with two faces tinted and no solid is produced

answer_key.worked: A cross shaped six square net folds into a cube, and the two arm ends become opposite faces.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the net's adjacency: the solid it makes, which faces meet, and whether it can close.
answer_key.precision: The fold path is precomputed as a sequence of two dimensional affine transforms per face, with collision detection on the projected polygons. Face areas are preserved throughout.
answer_key.ground_truth: adjacency(net) = the face adjacency graph. solid(net) = the solid key when it closes, null otherwise. facePairs(net) = the map of which faces meet.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

play_modes: MEETING PAIR: mark two faces you think will meet, then fold and see whether they did.
COLLISION HUNT: build an arrangement that collides, and say which pair goes to the same place.
HALF FOLD: stop halfway and trace one face back to where it started on the flat net.
UNFOLD TEST: fold fully, unfold, and check that every face is back exactly where it began.
normal.parameter_freedom: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.

a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists so the class watches the SAME face arrive. The flat outline of every square stays drawn while the square itself travels into the solid, and the isometric edge is scaled so the drawn rhombus has exactly the flat square's area — the two pictures are one object seen twice, which is the whole of why a net can be read before it is cut.

Beat 2 is the argument, not a second demonstration. Nothing is folded differently; the same closed cube is shown with r1c2 and r3c2 marked, and the point is that those two were decided by the net's own joins long before the fold ran. Roll a cube along the straight strip with a finger while you say it: in a straight run of squares, the one that ends up opposite is the one you reach by skipping one.

Beat 3 carries the idea to the case that breaks it, and the drawing has to show BOTH halves or it teaches nothing: r1c4 and r3c2 stop short of the same place tinted red, AND the sixth cube face is outlined empty. Overlap alone reads as a near miss that a different order of folding might rescue; overlap plus a hole is the diagnosis. Say plainly that no order of folding can separate two faces sent to one place.

media.title: The Ant's Secret Shortcut
media.context: This hook opens the topic on shortest paths on a cuboid. Students know nets. The film must not measure any route and must not say which unfolding wins.
media.description: An ant sits on one corner of a closed box and wants a crumb on a far corner, crawling only along the surface. Going up and over looks obvious, and snipping the box open and flattening it turns the winding route into a straight line.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Find a shortest surface path on a cuboid by unfolding it into a net. Key teaching points: 1) A surface path is hard to compare in three dimensions. 2) Unfolding turns it into a path on flat paper. 3) On flat paper the shortest route is a straight line. 4) Different unfoldings give different candidates, so all must be checked. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often assume the shortest path runs along the edges. 2) Students often check only one unfolding. Pause points: 0:24, at the end of flatten it out: ask whether up and over is really shortest. 0:24, just before the open question: ask how many unfoldings the class would try. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what unfolding does to the path. After viewing, ask why more than one unfolding matters.

topics.summary: Unfolding a cuboid turns a surface path into a straight line whose length is a hypotenuse, and different unfoldings give different lengths, so all must be compared. The learner unfolds, computes the straight length, and picks the shortest.

content.text: On a flat sheet the shortest route between two points is a straight line. A cuboid is not flat, but its surface can be unfolded into a flat net without stretching, so distances on the surface are kept. When you unfold, a surface path becomes a straight line on the net, and its length is the slanted side of a right triangle: the square root of one leg squared plus the other leg squared. For example, legs of 9 and 12 give a length of 15. But a box can be unfolded in several ways, and each way gives a different straight line, so you must compare them and choose the shortest. A wrong unfolding sends the straight line outside the net, meaning it matches no real path on the box.

overview.goal: The student matches a solid to its three flat views, constructs a solid from views alone, and finds two solids with the same views.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground with a stack of identical cubes drawn in fixed isometric projection beside three small square grids labelled top, front and side. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class holds that the three views pin the solid down, and a cube is added where no view can see it to find out.
overview.concept: Three flat views record what a solid looks like from three directions, but they do not fix it. A cube directly behind another is hidden in every view that would reveal it, so more than one stack can produce the same three views. Producing the views from a solid is determined; producing the solid from views is not.
overview.purpose: The student matches a solid to its three flat views, constructs a solid from views alone, and finds two solids with the same views.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Stack left and the three views right on a wide frame, stack above views on a 390 px frame. Every cell and every cube position keeps a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not fill any view while a prediction is still open, and never store a view separately from the stack. A stored view could drift from the solid it claims to describe.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. A view shades a cell when at least one cube lies along that line of sight, so any number of cubes along that line produces the same shading. Adding a cube directly behind an existing one therefore changes no view. That is exactly why views under determine the solid, and finding two solids with the same views proves it by construction. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

Beat 2 fills the three views from the stack, each computed by projection. Beat 3 gives three views and builds a solid from them, then finds a second solid with the same views. conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the cube stack with all three view panels empty, and ask the class to say out loud how many cubes could be hidden from every direction. Commit the class number on the prediction pad. Targets the stack on a 3 by 3 base with the views empty. Never fill a view panel before the prediction is committed. Call 2. observationsAndConclusions.why: Each view shades a cell when anything at all lies along that line of sight, so a second cube along the same line adds nothing new to shade
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A cube dropped directly behind another leaves all three panels completely unchanged
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The views cannot report what they cannot distinguish, which is precisely why they under determine the solid

observationsAndConclusions.why: Both stacks occupy the same columns and reach the same heights along each viewing direction, and nothing else is recorded
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Two visibly different stacks sit side by side under one shared set of views
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Finding a second solid is a proof by construction, and it settles the question far better than an argument does

observationsAndConclusions.why: Projection is a computation that any stack supports, while a set of views may describe no stack whatsoever
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Going from the solid to the views never fails, and going the other way sometimes has no answer at all
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A determined direction and an undetermined direction are not two halves of one relationship

media.description: A stack of identical cubes stands in fixed isometric projection on a plain 3 by 3 ground plate, beside three small grids of unit squares captioned in words - top view, front view, side view (from the right). The stack is held only as its column heights, so a cube with nothing under it cannot exist and a placement one level up is refused with the reason on screen. The three views are never stored: they are recomputed from the stack every time, a cell shading whenever at least one cube stands along that direction, so a view can never drift from the solid it describes. The decisive move is a cube added directly behind another - the cube count ticks from 8 to 9 while every one of the three panels holds completely still - and the two stacks are then set side by side under ONE shared set of views, which is the whole non-uniqueness argument in a single picture. Read-out chips carry the cube count, the shaded cells in each panel, the largest stack the same views allow and how many cubes can still hide. In Free Play the student adds and removes cubes by tapping a column, shades any view cell by hand and presses Check views, which names the panel that disagrees rather than merely refusing. Practice serves six items drawn from a thirty item pool on a difficulty ladder, each rendering the stack its own question describes, with the count, the largest and the slack all held back until the answer is checked.

concept.notation: The three views are the top, front and side, each drawn as a small grid of shaded cells. A view is a projection: it records whether anything is present along that line of sight.
concept.statement: Three flat views record what a solid looks like from three directions, but they do not fix it. A cube directly behind another is hidden in every view that would reveal it, so more than one stack can produce the same three views. Producing the views from a solid is determined; producing the solid from views is not.
misconceptions: Hidden cubes ignored, so the smallest stack is assumed to be the only one.
Views assumed to determine the solid uniquely.
concept.why_it_is_true: A view shades a cell when at least one cube lies along that line of sight, so any number of cubes along that line produces the same shading. Adding a cube directly behind an existing one therefore changes no view. That is exactly why views under determine the solid, and finding two solids with the same views proves it by construction.
worked_numbers: A stack of 4 cubes and one of 5 can share all three views.
The top view alone can hide any number of cubes below the top layer.
Three views of a 2 by 2 by 2 arrangement do not distinguish 7 cubes from 8.

A crowd seen from the side, where a tall person hides a shorter one exactly

A queue seen from directly above, showing positions but no heights

A building seen from the street, with a wing behind it that never appears

addCubeOutcomes.beside: all three views change, because a new column has been started
addCubeOutcomes.onFloor: the top view gains a shaded cell and the cube count rises
addCubeOutcomes.floating: refused with a reason, since a cube with nothing under it is not a stack the views describe
addCubeOutcomes.behindCube: the cube count rises and not one of the three views changes
addCubeOutcomes.onTopOfCube: the front and side views gain height while the top view is unchanged

shadeCellOutcomes.top: the cell shades when any column at that position holds at least one cube, whatever its height
shadeCellOutcomes.side: the cell shades when any cube sits at that depth and height, whatever its distance across
shadeCellOutcomes.front: the cell shades when any cube sits at that column and height, whatever its depth

checkViewsOutcomes.noneMatch: no panel takes a tick and the tool names all three as disagreeing
checkViewsOutcomes.allThreeMatch: each panel takes a tick and the build counts as a solution, without claiming to be the only one
checkViewsOutcomes.topOnlyMatches: the top panel takes a tick and the other two are named as disagreeing

setGridSizeOutcomes.1: a single column, where the views determine the solid completely
setGridSizeOutcomes.3: the standard base, where hidden cubes first become possible
setGridSizeOutcomes.4: the largest base, with the most room for a cube nothing can see

answer_key.worked: Three views do not fix the solid, because a cube directly behind another changes none of them.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the actual stack: the three views by projection, and whether a built stack matches a given view set.
answer_key.precision: The stack is a three dimensional boolean occupancy array rendered only through a fixed isometric projection function. The three views are recomputed from the stack every time and never stored.
answer_key.ground_truth: views(stack) = the three projections along each axis. matches(stack, views) = every view agrees. alternativeStack(views) = a different occupancy with the same views, when one exists.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Changes no view, which is the whole point, and the tool says so rather than treating it as an error.

edge_cases.case: A view set with more than one solid

Refused with the reason on screen, since a cube with nothing beneath it could not stand.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example adding a hidden cube a child suggests and showing no view changes.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

tool_config.tool_objective: The student matches a solid to its three flat views, constructs a solid from views alone, and finds two solids with the same views.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to fix what a view actually records. Point at one column of the stack and then at the single cell it shades, and say the rule in the class's own words: the cell is shaded because SOMETHING stands along that direction, not because of how much. The three shaded counts - 5, 6 and 6 - are on screen so the class can check the claim against the picture rather than take it.

Beat 2 is the whole argument, and it is a NON-EVENT, so it has to be staged long enough to be noticed. The cube count moves from 8 to 9 and not one of the eighteen cells changes. Ask for the change out loud BEFORE moving on, then let the class see there is none. Students who count only what they can see will have said 8; the count chip settles it.

Beat 3 turns the observation into a proof by construction. Two visibly different stacks, 8 cubes and 10, stand under ONE set of views with both counts printed. Say 'similar views' never 'the same solid', and resist arguing the point - the picture is the argument. The 2 in the Can hide chip is exactly the gap the views leave open, and it is countable, not vague.

media.title: Three Shadows That Rebuild a Solid
media.context: This hook opens the topic on the three standard views. Students know that one view is not enough. The film must not work out any view and must not say when three views fail.
media.description: Stack some identical cubes into a little sculpture and look at it from the front, from the top and from one side. Each direction gives a flat outline where a cube tucked directly behind another simply disappears.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Read and produce the front, top and side views of a stack of cubes. Key teaching points: 1) Each view is a flat outline from one direction. 2) A cube directly behind another does not appear. 3) The three standard views are front, top and side. 4) Some different stacks share all three views. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often count hidden cubes in a view. 2) Students often assume three views always fix the solid. Pause points: 0:22, at the end of hidden cubes vanish: ask how many squares the front view will hold. 0:22, just before the open question: ask what happens to a cube directly behind another. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask which three views engineers use. After viewing, ask whether three views are always enough.

topics.summary: A stack of cubes casts three views, each an outline that takes the tallest cube along a line of sight, and three views need not fix a unique stack. The learner reads the three views and finds the least and greatest cube counts for given views.

content.text: Every stack of cubes casts three flat views: the front view (looking from the front), the top view (looking straight down), and the side view (looking from one side). Each view is an outline, like a shadow, so a cube hidden directly behind another does not add to it. For the front view, each width column shows only its tallest cube, so you add the tallest heights across the width. The side view works the same way looking along the width. The top view shows every floor cell that has at least one cube, no matter how tall the stack. So a vertical tower of 4 cubes is 4 squares from the front and side but only 1 square from the top.

content.text: Three views carry a lot of information, but they are still only outlines, and an outline hides any cube tucked directly behind another. So a hidden cube can be there or not there without changing the front, top or side view. This means different stacks can share all three views. For a front 2 by 2 square, a side 2 by 2 square and a full 2 by 2 top view, the stack could have 6, 7 or 8 cubes: the least is 6, with two tall stacks on a diagonal, and the most is 8, with every cell 2 cubes tall. Some views do pin a unique solid, such as a single tower or a plain row, but in general you can only give the least and greatest possible number of cubes.

Three views carry a lot of information, but they are still only outlines, and an outline hides any cube tucked directly behind another. So a hidden cube can be there or not there without changing the front, top or side view. This means different stacks can share all three views. For a front 2 by 2 square, a side 2 by 2 square and a full 2 by 2 top view, the stack could have 6, 7 or 8 cubes: the least is 6, with two tall stacks on a diagonal, and the most is 8, with every cell 2 cubes tall. Some views do pin a unique solid, such as a single tower or a plain row, but in general you can only give the least and greatest possible number of cubes.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer how a stack of identical cubes casts a front, a top and a side outline, and determine that the front and side take the tallest stack along each line of sight while the top marks every covered floor cell. They will explain why a cube hidden behind another adds nothing to an outline, and count the unit squares in each of the three views.
Examine the worked examples of reading the three views, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving reading the three views, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer why three views can still leave a stack uncertain, and determine that a cube hidden directly behind another can be present or absent without changing any outline, so different stacks can share all three views. They will explain how to find the least and the greatest number of cubes that are consistent with a given set of front, top and side views.
