media.title: Drawing Cubes That Cannot Exist
media.context: This hook opens the topic on isometric drawing. Students can read views. The film must not say what makes a drawing buildable and must not analyse the impossible figure.
media.description: On a slanted grid with three equal directions, a single cube drawn corner on shows three faces at once and looks convincingly solid. The same neat rules let a clever artist draw a staircase that climbs forever.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Draw solids on an isometric grid and recognise figures that cannot be built. Key teaching points: 1) An isometric grid has three equally spaced directions. 2) A cube drawn corner on shows three faces. 3) Stacked cubes make a convincing solid drawing. 4) Locally correct corners do not guarantee a buildable object. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often trust a drawing because each corner looks right. 2) Students often draw isometric cubes with unequal directions. Pause points: 0:23, at the end of or a staircase to nowhere: ask what makes the staircase impossible. 0:23, just before the open question: ask how many faces one drawn cube shows. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what an isometric grid gives you. After viewing, ask whether a perfect drawing must be buildable.

media.description: A 100-second animation. Seconds 0 to 30 show a cube rotating until it rests on one corner with the opposite corner directly above. content.text: An isometric grid has three edge directions: the vertical stands for height, and two slanted directions stand for length and depth, all with equal unit lengths. A single cube drawn corner-on shows 3 faces and 9 edges, with 3 edges hidden at the back. You draw a solid edge by edge, counting units along each axis, so a block that is length by depth by height contains that many unit cubes, for example 3 by 2 by 1 is 6 cubes. Isometric drawings communicate shape well because parallel edges stay parallel and equal lengths stay equal. But be careful: a figure can be drawn so that every corner looks fine, yet the whole thing cannot be built, like the impossible triangle, which secretly joins two beams that are really at different depths.

topics.detailed_summary: On an isometric grid, solids are drawn along three equal axes of length, depth and height, with parallel edges staying parallel, and some figures like the impossible triangle can be drawn but not built. The learner draws, counts cubes and edges, and spots impossible figures.
topics.publication_chunk: An isometric grid has three edge directions: the vertical stands for height, and two slanted directions stand for length and depth, all with equal unit lengths. A single cube drawn corner-on shows 3 faces and 9 edges, with 3 edges hidden at the back. You draw a solid edge by edge, counting units along each axis, so a block that is length by depth by height contains that many unit cubes, for example 3 by 2 by 1 is 6 cubes. Isometric drawings communicate shape well because parallel edges stay parallel and equal lengths stay equal. But be careful: a figure can be drawn so that every corner looks fine, yet the whole thing cannot be built, like the impossible triangle, which secretly joins two beams that are really at different depths. objectives.strand_name: Fractals: shapes that repeat at every scale
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what stays the same when a fern or a coastline is magnified, and determine that a self-similar shape is built from smaller copies of the whole made by one rule repeated at smaller and smaller scales. They will explain that a plain smooth ball or straight line holds no such copy, and predict how the number of copies multiplies at every step.

objectives.strand_name: Fractals: shapes that repeat at every scale
objectives.objective_text: Examine the worked examples of self-similar shapes, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: Fractals: shapes that repeat at every scale
objectives.objective_text: Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving self-similar shapes, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: Fractals: shapes that repeat at every scale
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer why the Sierpinski carpet keeps more squares than it removes, and determine that cutting each square into 9 and dropping the centre leaves 8 survivors, so the count multiplies by 8 each step and equals 8 raised to the step number. They will explain that the squares removed at a step match the number that remained the step before.

objectives.strand_name: Fractals: shapes that repeat at every scale
objectives.objective_text: Examine the worked examples of counting the squares that remain, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: Fractals: shapes that repeat at every scale
objectives.objective_text: Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving counting the squares that remain, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: Fractals: shapes that repeat at every scale
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer why the carpet fills with holes yet still holds squares, and determine that every surviving square opens one new hole while old holes stay, so the total is a running sum of 1 plus 8 plus 64 and onward. They will explain that keeping 8 of 9 parts multiplies the leftover area by 8/9 each step, so the area shrinks toward zero even as the squares grow.

objectives.strand_name: Fractals: shapes that repeat at every scale
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what joining the midpoints of an equilateral triangle produces, and determine that it makes 4 equal triangles, so removing the middle one leaves 3 and multiplies the count by 3 each step to reach 3 raised to the step number. They will explain that each survivor keeps 3 of its 4 equal parts, so the leftover area is multiplied by 3/4 and heads toward zero.

objectives.strand_name: Fractals: shapes that repeat at every scale
objectives.objective_text: Examine the worked examples of counting triangles in the gasket, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: Fractals: shapes that repeat at every scale
objectives.objective_text: Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving counting triangles in the gasket, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: Fractals: shapes that repeat at every scale
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer why a Koch side becomes four segments and not three, and determine that dividing a side into 3 equal parts and raising a bump on the middle replaces one side with 4, so the number of sides multiplies by 4 each step. They will explain that starting from a triangle's 3 sides, the count after n steps equals 3 multiplied by 4 raised to n.

objectives.strand_name: Fractals: shapes that repeat at every scale
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer why the Koch boundary lengthens without ever escaping a small region, and determine that each step multiplies the number of sides by 4 while each side becomes one third as long, so the perimeter is multiplied by 4/3 every step. They will explain that because 4/3 is greater than 1, the perimeter grows past any value while the whole figure stays bounded.

objectives.strand_name: Fractals: shapes that repeat at every scale
objectives.objective_text: Examine the worked examples of the perimeter that grows forever, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: Fractals: shapes that repeat at every scale
objectives.objective_text: Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving the perimeter that grows forever, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer why one solid can look completely different when it is turned, and determine that seeing a solid means seeing its outline from a single direction, so different viewpoints give different outlines. They will explain that an outline cannot fix the solid, since a circle could come from a sphere, a cylinder or a cone, and a triangle from a cone, a pyramid or a prism.

Students will be able to infer how flat surfaces, meeting lines and corner points describe a solid, and determine that a face is a flat surface, an edge is where two faces meet, and a vertex is where edges meet, hidden ones included. They will explain that for such solids the number of faces plus vertices minus edges always equals 2, and predict a missing count from the other two.
Examine the worked examples of counting faces, edges and vertices, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving counting faces, edges and vertices, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer how the counts of a prism or a pyramid depend on the base polygon, and determine that a prism on an n-sided base has n plus 2 faces, 3n edges and 2n vertices, while a pyramid has n plus 1 faces, 2n edges and n plus 1 vertices. They will explain why naming a solid by its base predicts these counts for any base size without building it.

Students will be able to infer why six squares are not enough to guarantee a cube, and determine which flat arrangements fold shut and which fail because two faces overlap or a face stays open. They will explain that a cube has exactly 11 distinct nets, a regular tetrahedron only 2 and a regular octahedron 11, counting two arrangements as the same when a rotation or a flip matches them.
Examine the worked examples of which arrangements fold into a cube, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving which arrangements fold into a cube, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer why a bug's shortest route over a box is easier to find on a flat unfolding, and determine that once unfolded the path becomes a straight line whose length is the square root of the sum of the squares of the two legs. They will explain that different unfoldings give different straight lengths, so every unfolding must be compared to select the shortest.
Examine the worked examples of unfolding to straighten the path, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving unfolding to straighten the path, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer how a stack of identical cubes casts a front, a top and a side outline, and determine that the front and side take the tallest stack along each line of sight while the top marks every covered floor cell. They will explain why a cube hidden behind another adds nothing to an outline, and count the unit squares in each of the three views.
Examine the worked examples of reading the three views, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving reading the three views, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer why three views can still leave a stack uncertain, and determine that a cube hidden directly behind another can be present or absent without changing any outline, so different stacks can share all three views. They will explain how to find the least and the greatest number of cubes that are consistent with a given set of front, top and side views.

Students will be able to infer how three equal axes of length, depth and height place unit cubes on an isometric grid, and determine that a block counted along each axis holds that many cubes while a corner-on cube shows 3 faces and some hidden edges. They will explain that a figure can be drawn consistently at every corner yet be impossible to build when its parts could never meet in space.

summary_stats.counts_note: One distinct tool per concept; each tool runs four mods (AI demo, Learn, Practice, Free Play), with one objective each for AI demo, Learn and Practice and none for Free Play.
summary_stats.videos_note: One 30 to 40 second curiosity hook video per topic, plus a chapter intro video and a chapter summary video of 1 to 2 minutes each.
summary_stats.tool_needed_note: Per-item boolean for how the ANSWER is entered, NOT whether to show the tool. The frontend ALWAYS renders the tool. true = the answer must be produced through the tool. false = the student reasons it out (typed/spoken) and the tool stays on screen as an aid.
summary_stats.solved_examples_note: Each solved example carries a first-person 'reasoning' field that generalises the method.
summary_stats.practice_problems_note: 198 practice items in all = (14 microconcepts x 10 tool-answered) + (14 x 4 reasoning items) + 2 proof items on the concepts that state a general claim.
summary_stats.question_repository_note: Worked-example and practice questions are no longer inline. Each learn/practice concept carries a question_bank_ref into question_repository.json; the teacher agent pulls questions from the repository at teach time. The teaching (AI-demo) concept keeps its inline source_ai_reasoning block.

authoring_rules.nesting: Each objective contains exactly one concept; each concept contains its solved examples then its practice questions.
authoring_rules.solved_examples: At least 10 per microconcept; each is demonstrated on that section's tool with numbered steps, a final answer and first-person reasoning that models how to think, not just which buttons to press.
authoring_rules.practice_questions: At least 10 tool-answered items per microconcept (marked right/wrong on the tool), followed by exactly 4 reasoning items: application, reverse, explain, error_spotting. A concept that states a general claim carries a 5th reasoning item, proof, between explain and error_spotting.

mods.does: The AI teaches the whole concept and works the higher-order reasoning questions (application, reverse, explain, error-spotting) with full step-by-step explanations, with the tool on screen; the student only watches.
The AI demonstrates the worked examples one step at a time on the tool.
The student answers the tool-answered practice questions that reinforce the worked examples.
The student freely solves any question of the same kind on the tool, neither taught nor scored.
